Title 3— 
The President 
Executive Order 13900 of December 17, 2019 
Providing for the Closing of Executive Departments and 
Agencies of the Federal Government on December 24, 2019 
By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the 
laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered as follows: 
Section 1. All executive departments and agencies of the Federal Government 
shall be closed and their employees excused from duty on Tuesday, December 
24, 2019, the day before Christmas Day. 
Sec. 2. The heads of executive departments and agencies may determine 
that certain offices and installations of their organizations, or parts thereof, 
must remain open and that certain employees must report for duty on 
December 24, 2019, for reasons of national security, defense, or other public 
need. 
Sec. 3. December 24, 2019, shall be considered as falling within the scope 
of Executive Order 11582 of February 11, 1971, and of 5 U.S.C. 5546 and 
6103(b) and other similar statutes insofar as they relate to the pay and 
leave of employees of the United States. 
Sec. 4. The Director of the Office of Personnel Management shall take 
such actions as may be necessary to implement this order. 
Sec. 5. General Provisions. (a) This order shall be implemented consistent 
with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations. 
(b) Nothing in this order shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect: 
(i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, 
or the head thereof; or 
(ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget 
relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 13900 of December 17, 2019 (84 FR 69983, Federal Register issue of December 20, 2019) closed executive departments and agencies and excused their employees from duty on Tuesday, December 24, 2019, the day before Christmas Day, with agency-head discretion to keep offices open, treatment of that day under Executive Order 11582 and 5 U.S.C. 5546 and 6103(b) for pay and leave, an OPM implementation direction, and general provisions. Every provision is confined to or tied to December 24, 2019, so each was exhausted by its own terms when that day ended. The end is recorded as December 24, 2019 inclusive; the exclusive reading (ending when the day begins) is the alternative. No held instrument revokes, extends or amends the order. The working text is the official Federal Register page text (machine-extracted from the PDF), not an authenticated transcription. The dossier's note that the target provision in Executive Order 11582 is not located is not an ending: section 3 only cites that 1971 order, which cannot revoke a later one.

Executive Order 13965 of December 11, 2020 (85 FR 81337, Federal Register issue of December 16, 2020) closed executive departments and agencies and excused their employees from duty on Thursday, December 24, 2020, the day before Christmas Day, with agency-head discretion to keep offices open, treatment of that day under Executive Order 11582 and 5 U.S.C. 5546 and 6103(b) for pay and leave, an OPM implementation direction, and general provisions. Every provision is confined to or tied to December 24, 2020, so each was exhausted by its own terms when that day ended. The end is recorded as December 24, 2020 inclusive; the exclusive reading (ending when the day begins) is the alternative. No held instrument revokes, extends or amends the order. The working text is the official Federal Register page text (machine-extracted from the PDF), not an authenticated transcription. The dossier's note that the target provision in Executive Order 11582 is not located is not an ending: section 3 only cites that 1971 order, which cannot revoke a later one.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The sole paragraph revokes Executive Order No. 8323 of January 22, 1940 (the abolition of Customs Collection District No. 43 (Tennessee), the revocation of the Memphis, Chattanooga and Nashville port designations, and the extensions of District Nos. 42 and 45) and says the earlier order "is hereby revoked." It is a self-executing one-time act with no later effective date, condition or continuing duty, so it was performed and exhausted when the President signed it on February 8, 1940 (the signature block reads "February 8, 1940."; filed February 9, 1940; Federal Register issue of February 10, 1940). The effect of the revocation survives as an accrued consequence, but the command is spent. No later instrument in the held record revokes, amends or restates this order. This is an own-terms end by performance, not an inference from a later cleanup instrument.

The loss of port-of-entry status is a surviving consequence of that executed act, not a continuing command. No instrument held in the repository revokes, amends or restores the designation by executive order.
